core: The working definition, attributed: financial ratios are calculations that compare two or more figures from a company's financial statements to measure performance and financial health (CFI Financial Ratios); ratios also make it easier to compare businesses of different sizes and track results over time

The three finance questions, one line each: liquidity (can it pay near-term bills?), profitability (is it earning enough?), leverage (how much debt?); the accounting subject owns the formulas — referenced only, not taught here
The decision uses, one line each: lenders assess ability to repay, investors assess returns and risk, managers track operations
The comparison practice, stated simply: a ratio alone means little; ratios earn meaning compared over time (trends) and against peers (benchmarks)
The limits, the honest note: accounting rules shape the numbers the ratios are built from, and past results do not equal future results
Ratios and valuation: ratios feed judgments of value (P/E and related multiples); the finance subject's valuation topics (stocks, return, risk) reference this
The honest framing, the reality check: ratios are the language of financial judgment — a lens, not a verdict
supporting: CFI's category map: liquidity ratios = short-term payment ability; leverage ratios = debt and capital structure; profitability ratios = profit relative to sales, assets, or equity; market value ratios = valuation and investor returns; efficiency ratios = asset use and productivity

CFI's who-uses section: external users (investors, equity research analysts, lenders, creditors) and internal users (management, corporate finance teams); lenders and creditors rely on ratios to determine creditworthiness and set appropriate interest rates for loans; investors analyze ratios to monitor financial performance and evaluate the success of their investment; management teams use ratio insights to identify operational strengths and weaknesses, set performance targets, and make strategic decisions

CFI's comparison guidance: analysts rarely rely on a single ratio; they use combinations of ratios to track performance trends, benchmark against peers, and identify potential risks or strengths; a single ratio gives only one piece of information
CFI's trend analysis: comparing a company's figures across multiple reporting periods to evaluate whether performance is improving, declining, or remaining stable
The four classic ratios named as the accounting subject's formulas: current ratio (liquidity), profit margin and return on equity (profitability), debt-to-equity (leverage) — reference only

OpenStax Principles of Finance 11.1: the P/E ratio (price an investor must pay for every unit of current or future corporate earnings) as one of the most consistently used calculations in company and common-stock evaluation, with P/B and P/S as alternative valuation multipliers
OpenStax Principles of Finance 17.1: the debt a firm uses is often referred to as financial leverage; companies typically finance assets through a mix of equity and debt

OpenStax Principles of Finance 4.1: accrual accounting records revenues when earned and expenses when incurred rather than when cash moves — the reported figures that ratios are built from are shaped by accounting rules

OpenStax Principles of Finance 15.1: the return may not be what the investor was expecting; this uncertainty about what the return will be is referred to as risk — past-reported ratios cannot guarantee future results

claims.claim: Financial ratios are calculations that compare two or more figures from a company's financial statements to measure performance and financial health; ratios also make it easier to compare businesses of different sizes and track results over time.

The main categories of financial ratios are liquidity ratios (short-term payment ability), leverage ratios (debt and capital structure), efficiency ratios (asset use and productivity), profitability ratios (profit relative to sales, assets, or equity), and market value ratios (valuation and investor returns).

Financial ratio analysis is used by external stakeholders — investors, equity research analysts, lenders, and creditors — and internal users such as management and corporate finance teams; lenders and creditors rely on ratios to determine creditworthiness and set appropriate interest rates for loans, investors analyze ratios to monitor financial performance and evaluate the success of their investment, and management teams use ratio insights to identify operational strengths and weaknesses, set performance targets, and make strategic decisions.

Analysts rarely rely on a single ratio; they use combinations of ratios to track a company's performance trends, benchmark it against peers, and identify potential risks or strengths, because a single ratio gives only one piece of information about a company's financial picture.
Trend analysis compares a company's financial data across multiple reporting periods to evaluate whether performance is improving, declining, or remaining stable.

The current ratio is a key liquidity ratio measuring a company's ability to cover its short-term liabilities; net profit margin measures profit relative to sales; return on equity measures how effectively a company uses shareholders' equity to generate profit; and the debt-to-equity ratio shows how a company's capital structure is tilted toward debt or equity financing. The accounting subject owns these formulas; this lesson references them only.

The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio — the price an investor must pay for every unit of current (or future) corporate earnings — is one of the most consistently used calculations in company and common-stock evaluation; price-to-book and price-to-sales are alternative valuation multipliers.
The debt a firm uses is often referred to as financial leverage; companies typically finance assets through a mix of equity (selling ownership shares) and debt (borrowing from lenders).
Accrual accounting records revenues when earned and expenses when incurred rather than when cash moves, so the reported figures that ratios are built from are shaped by accounting rules and choices.

The return an investor receives may not be what was expected — this uncertainty about what the return will be is what finance calls risk — so ratios built from past reported figures cannot guarantee future results.

conflictingEvidence: None found across the sources used. CFI's Financial Ratios page lists five categories (liquidity, leverage, efficiency, profitability, market value), while this lesson leads with the three finance questions decision-makers most often ask (liquidity, profitability, leverage) and touches efficiency and market value in passing — a difference of emphasis, not of substance. The subject division of labor is deliberate and consistent with the sibling topics: the accounting subject's financial-ratios lesson owns the four formulas and their preparation (current ratio, profit margin, return on equity, debt-to-equity), while this finance lesson uses the ratios as decision tools and references the accounting lessons rather than teaching the math.
rightsIssues: All sources used reference-only; no source prose reproduced. OpenStax pages were read live via HTTP (openstax.org serves full content in the initial HTML for these sections); CFI pages read live via HTTP. Working definition attributed to CFI and restated in original prose.
